query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing tantalum (Ta) with niobium (Nb) in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower the alloy's density while preserving its high-strength mechanical properties at both room temperature and approximately 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast HfMoTaTiZr produced by arc‐melting synthesis, with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and high strength at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Systematic substitution of Ta with Nb to form a new alloy composition (HfMoNbTiZr) via arc‐melting synthesis.
generation.conditions: Samples produced in the as‐cast condition and tested under tensile and/or compressive loading at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a similar solid solution phase (likely BCC or similar high-entropy solid solution structure) that supports both light-weighting due to Nb's lower atomic mass and the maintenance of high-temperature strength.
generation.mechanism: Niobium, having a lower atomic density compared to tantalum, reduces the overall alloy density when substituted, while its refractory nature ensures that the stability and high strength of the alloy continue to be maintained up to around 1000 °C. The elemental substitution is expected to minimally affect the favorable phase structure responsible for mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduction in density (expected directional decrease) relative to 10.21 g/cm³ with comparable yield strength and ductility at both room temperature and ~1000 °C; precise quantitative reduction is uncertain but likely in the range of a moderate percent decrease.
generation.baseline: Properties of as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr: high strength at room temperature and elevated temperatures with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to the as‐cast condition with mechanical testing performed at room temperature and under high-temperature conditions near 1000 °C, where both strength and ductility must meet or exceed the baseline performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact percentage reduction in density and the detailed influence of Nb substitution on microstructural features (which may subtly alter the mechanical response) remain uncertain. Additionally, potential changes in high-temperature oxidation resistance were not directly addressed by this intervention.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples via arc-melting synthesis: one set of the baseline HfMoTaTiZr and one set of the modified HfMoNbTiZr (with Ta substituted by Nb in equiatomic proportions). Perform density measurements using the Archimedes method and conduct tensile or compressive tests at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C under identical loading conditions.
measurements: Ductility (percentage elongation or similar metric) at both temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HfMoNbTiZr alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in density relative to HfMoTaTiZr OR if the mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) at room temperature and 1000 °C are degraded by more than an acceptable margin (e.g., exceeding a 10% drop compared to baseline values), then the hypothesis that Ta substitution with Nb successfully reduces density while retaining mechanical performance is rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. chosen.why: This move most directly addresses the open question by reducing density via a targeted composition change while leveraging well-established alloy synthesis and testing techniques to ensure that the high strength at both ambient and elevated temperatures is maintained.
